opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the question is usually framed the wrong way. People imagine there's a training phase where the knowledge goes in, and then a deployment phase where it's used, and so "retaining" means not forgetting what was put in during training. But that's not how any animal works, and it's not how I think a real intelligent agent should work. For a continually learning system, there's just experience: a stream of observations, actions, and rewards. And everything the agent knows has to come from that stream and be maintained by that stream.

So where does the information go? It goes into a few places. It goes into the policy, what you do in each situation. It goes into the value function, how well you expect things to go from here. And, importantly, it goes into the state representation and the model of the world: your predictions about what will happen if you do this or that. Those are all just weights, parameters being adjusted by learning as you go. There's no separate memory bank where facts get filed away. The knowledge *is* the predictions.

Now, the hard part, and I don't want to minimize it, is that our current methods are not good at this. Deep learning, as we use it, has what we call catastrophic forgetting, and maybe more seriously, a loss of plasticity. If you keep training a network on a changing stream, it gradually loses the ability to learn new things at all. We've shown this pretty clearly. The networks were designed for a one-time training regime, and when you ask them to keep learning forever, they degrade. So that's a real problem, and it's one of the things I think the field has neglected because everyone's been focused on the big pre-training approach.

What do you do about it? Part of it is algorithmic. Things like continually injecting variability, reinitializing the units that aren't contributing, what we've called continual backprop. Part of it is having learning rates that adapt per weight, so the system learns which parts of its knowledge are stable and should be protected, and which parts need to keep moving. That's meta-learning in a simple, practical sense. And part of it is about generalization: you want representations where learning something new transfers well and doesn't trample what came before. We don't really have good automated methods for ensuring that yet. Right now, when these systems generalize well, it's mostly because the researchers sculpted it that way.

But the deeper point is this: the world is big, much bigger than the agent. You can never pre-load everything the agent will need. Each agent will encounter its own particular situation: its own job, its own people, its own idiosyncrasies. That knowledge has to be learned on the job and retained on the job. So retention isn't an add-on. It's the central capability. An agent that can't do that isn't really learning from experience, and learning from experience is, I think, what intelligence fundamentally is.

r001.rationale: The response says continual learning updates the system’s weights and rejects a separate memory bank, but it does not distinguish that from information held in an LLM’s context window.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the retention isn't a separate thing from the learning. People sometimes imagine there's a learning process and then a storage process, like you learn something and then you file it away somewhere. But in a continually learning agent, the knowledge just is the weights, the parameters of the function approximator, and those get changed a little bit on every step. So the question of how it retains information is really the question of how it keeps from overwriting what it already knows when it learns something new.

And I'd say that's the big unsolved problem, honestly. We know how to learn. We've known how to learn for decades, temporal-difference learning, gradient descent, all of that. What we don't know how to do well is learn for a long time. If you run a deep learning system continually, the way an animal lives continually, it loses plasticity. It gets worse at learning new things. And it also forgets, catastrophically sometimes. Those two problems, loss of plasticity and catastrophic forgetting, are really the same problem seen from two sides. The network is using all its capacity on what it learned early, and then it has nowhere to put the new stuff, or it puts it on top of the old stuff.

The way I think about retaining knowledge is in terms of what the knowledge is about. In my view, the knowledge of an agent should be predictions, predictions about what will happen to its sensations and its rewards if it behaves in certain ways. Those are grounded. You can check them against experience. And a prediction that keeps being confirmed, you shouldn't need to keep relearning it. The error signal is zero, so the weights don't move. That's actually a very natural form of retention. The things that are true and keep being true stay in place, because nothing is pushing them out. The things that stop being true get revised. That's what you want.

The harder part is making sure the parts of the network that encode the stable knowledge are protected while other parts are free to change. We've been looking at ideas like continual backprop, where you keep reinitializing the units that aren't contributing anything, so there's always some fresh capacity available to learn with, while the useful units are left alone. I don't think that's the final answer. But I think it's the right kind of answer. It's a mechanism inside the learning process itself, not a bolt-on memory module.

And I'd add one more thing. We shouldn't think of memory as the main thing. Animals don't carry around a copy of their experience. They carry around a changed way of behaving and a changed way of predicting. The experience is gone. What's retained is the competence. So when you ask how a continually learning system retains what it gains, I'd say, it doesn't retain the information. It retains the change in itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes retained knowledge as changes to a continually learning agent’s weights, but it does not distinguish that from information held in a large language model’s context window.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a change in the agent, rather than necessarily as a record of what happened. An experience comes along, and it changes your policy, your predictions, perhaps your model of the world. Those changes are what you carry forward. You don’t have to remember the particular experience in order to benefit from it.

And there’s a tension there, because you want to retain what you’ve learned, but you also want to remain able to change. The world may change, or you may discover that your earlier understanding was wrong. So retaining everything unchanged isn’t the objective. The objective is to carry forward what helps you predict and act, while continuing to learn from the next experience.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning as changes to an agent’s policy, predictions, or world model, but it does not distinguish information in an LLM’s context window from information incorporated into a system’s weights.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to distinguish retaining experience from retaining what you’ve learned from experience. You don’t necessarily want a record of everything that happened. You want your experience to change your predictions and your way of behaving, so that the next time you encounter a similar situation, you do better.

In reinforcement learning, some of that information is in the value function: what consequences do I expect if I’m in this situation, or if I take this action? Some is in the policy, and some might be in a model of how the world works. Those are different ways of carrying the effects of the past forward.

And retention isn’t quite the whole objective, because the world can change. Something you learned earlier may no longer be true. So a continually learning system has to preserve useful knowledge while remaining able to revise it. You don’t want learning to be something that happens once and then stops. It’s part of the ongoing interaction with the world.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes stored experience from learned effects, but it does not mention or distinguish an LLM’s context window from information incorporated into model weights.
